subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-PURCHASES FROM THE UNITED STATES

speechtext:
Mr. LaVERGNE:
1.	Is the government aware that the Canadian National Railways manufacture their cars, bolts, hinges, radios, keys, and many other articles, used in their railway system, in the United States?
2.	Is the government aware that many of the said articles show the commercial mark "Made in U.S.A.?"
3.	Is it the intention of the government to remedy this state of affairs by having the Canadian National Railways manufacture said articles in Canada?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-PURCHASES FROM THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The Canadian National Railways do not manufacture in the United States cars, bolts, hinges, radios, keys, or other articles used in

Questions
their railway system. Its equipment requirements for United States lines are purchased from car and locomotive builders in the United States. Radio and receiving sets purchased by the railways are manufactured in Canada, at Toronto and Montreal.
The policy of the government and its instructions are that the requirements of the railway shall be filled from Canadian sources, and the Canadian National management states that it is the practice of the railway to purchase in Canada all equipment, materials and articles which can be manufactured in this country. All contracts for locomotives, car equipment, buildings, etc., provide that Canadian materials must be used in their manufacture and construction, and the railway management state that considerably over ninety per cent of its total purchases are from Canadian manufacturers and wholesalers.

In the matter of temporary appointments to the civil service' pending a permanent appointment under the certificate of the Civil Service Commission, what is the mode of procedure adopted by the various departments of government ?

A uniform practice is authorized throughout the various departments of the government, as follows: when a vacancy occurs the department sends a requisition to the commission to fill the same. If there is an eligible list established in the commission for this class of vacancy, an assignment is made forthwith. If there is no list of eligibles, the commission advertises a competition for the purpose of establishing an eligible list, and in the meantime the department is granted local selection for temporary employment pending the filling of the position permanently as a result of the competition. A temporary certificate is then issued by the commission covering the temporary appointment until the permanent assignment is made.
In the past there has been abuse by the departments in connection with these acting appointments. The Civil Service Commissioners have reported on it in their annual reports from time to time and in the report for the calendar year 1928, at page 8, reported as follows:
"Acting appointments:
"In their last report the commissioners drew attention to the practice, which has frequently been found to exist, of placing officers in vacant positions in an acting capacity for considerable periods of time before asking the commission to take steps to fill the vacancies either by promotion or by open competition. When the competition is finally held, the

Questions
temporary incumbent of the position has obviously an unfair advantage over the other competitors. The commission accordingly requests that requisitions for appointments or promotions be filed at as early a date as possible, so that when the position in question becomes vacant there will be no necessity for an acting appointment, but the new appointee will be ready to take over the duties."
In their annual report for 1929, the commissioners reported as follows on page 10: "Certificates necessary for acting appointments :
"In previous reports, the commissioners have had occasion to call attention to the delay on the part of departments in installing in office persons who have been certified for appointment, and the practice of retaining in their places persons for whose employment no legal authority exists. This difficulty has now been overcome, to a great extent, in one department at least, a ruling having been received from the law officers of the crown to the effect that a temporary certificate from the commission was required in the case of all persons placed in charge of revenue post offices, pending a permanent appointment. Under present procedure, the department, as in the past, installs a temporary incumbent in office as soon as a postmastership becomes vacant; but application is made immediately to the Civil Service Commission for a certificate of temporary employment for the person placed in charge, and the position is immediately advertised. The result is a greatly reduced delay in the making of the permanent appointment, and the installation of the properly certified candidate as soon as may be after the issue of the permanent certificate."
In order to expedite matters in connection with the filling of such vacancies as postmasterships, lightkeeperships and so forth, an arrangement has been arrived at between some of the departments and the commission, which permits the department to advertise the vacancy as soon as it occurs and to immediately advise the commission regarding its action, furnishing a copy of the poster. This practice is not always adhered to promptly.
When the establishment of a permanent position is pending, or when the outgoing incumbent of a position is given retiring leave, the commission is advised by the department and thereupon assigns temporarily the candidate, whose name being next on the eligible list, will automatically be permanently appointed when the permanent position is
established, or when the position officially becomes vacant through the expiration of the retiring leave of the late incumbent.
When the commission makes an assignment to a department, provision is made under Section 24 of the Civil Service Act for a probationary period during which time the deputy head of the department may ask for an extension of the period of probation or reject the assignee entirely. In the event of final rejection the candidate next on the list is assigned. In the absence of available eligibles a new competition is required.

Before the orders of the day are called perhaps it is expected that I should communicate to the house in a formal way the recognition by His Majesty's government in Canada of the provisional government in Spain. Hon. members will be aware that in the first step towards the return of constitutional government, municipal elections were held throughout Spain on April 12, being the first election since the establishment of the dictatorship in 1922. They resulted in an overwhelming victory for the Republicans in all the larger centres. A republic was proclaimed at Madrid with Senor Alcala Zamora as provisional president, and at other provincial centres. No resistance was offered by the supporters of the monarchy. The King of Spain left the country without formal abdication. The new government appears to have established its authority without disturbance. Following consultation between His Majesty's governments, recognition of the provisional government of the republic of Spain was accorded in notes delivered by His Majesty's ambassador at Madrid on April 22, on behalf of His Majesty's governments in the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and the Irish Free State. Recognition has also been accorded by some seventeen other countries, including France and the United States.

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Naturalization Act.
He saidl: In introducing this bill a few days ago, I suggested that it was not a bill which involved any partisan discussion, but was one which interested members on both sides of the house and in respect to which the government desired to have the best advice possible after careful consideration. In introducing the bill
FMr. Brown. 1
I called attention to the fact that section 13 of the Naturalization Act, chapter 138, Revised Statutes of Canada of 1927, provides that:
The wife of a British subject shall be deemed to be a British subject, and the wife of an alien shall be deemed to be an alien.
On that occasion I pointed out that it was obviously impracticable to regard a woman as having her alien husband's nationality if, according to the law of his country, she is deemed to be an alien in his country or elsewhere.
We have at present expressed certain exceptions in section 13 of the Naturalization Act. We have provided in subsection 2 that:
Where a man ceases during the continuance of his marriage to be a British subject, it shall be lawful for his wife to make a declaration that she desires to retain British nationality, and thereupon she shall be deemed to remain a British subject.
That exception we have still retained in subsection 3 of this bill. Subsection 3 of the existing section 13 is retained in subsection 5 of this bill with a slight change in the wording to make it conform to the terms of the proposed new amendment.
This amendment of the existing law in Canada is rendered more urgent in view of recent changes in the law of the United States of America. Until a short time ago the law of the United States was similar to the law which prevails in this country. Section 1994 of the act of the United States congress of February 10, 1855, provides that:
Any woman who is now or may hereafter be married to a citizen of the United States, and who might herself be 'awfully naturalized, shall be deemed a citizen.
That was the same principle which was embodied in the English law and introduced info our own Naturalization Act as the law of Canada.
Section 3 of the act of the congress of the United States of March 2, 1907, provided that:
Any American woman who marries a foreigner shall take the nationality of her husband.
That was the English law and the law of Canada. Those two provisions were in strict conformity with the original provisions of our law. But those two sections were repealed by sections 6 and 7 of the Cable act, which was enacted by United States congress on September 22, 1922. The Cable act enacted in section 2 thereof:
That any woman who marries a citizen of the United States after the passage of this act, or any woman whose husband is naturalized after the passage of this act, shall not become a citizen of the United States by reason of such marriage or naturalization, but, if eligible to

Naturalization Act
citizenship, she may be naturalized upon full and complete compliance with all the requirements of the naturalization laws.
That act contains certain exceptions, to which I shall now refer, in favour of speedier naturalization, which were further provided for in a subsequent amendment by a law of the United States congress passed on July 3, 1930. The Cable act of 1922 also provided that:
A woman citizen of the United States shall not cease to be a citizen by reason of her marriage unless she makes a formal renunciation of her citizenship before a court having jurisdiction over naturalization of aliens.
A woman who was a citizen of the United States upon her marriage with a British subject, thereby attained a dual nationality. With respect to that I am not for the present concerned. A woman, on the other hand, who was a British subject, upon her marriage with a citizen of the United States, thereby became stateless. She thereby lost her status as a British subject under our law without attaining the status of a citizen of the United States under the law which prevails in that country. So intimate are the social relations existing between Canada and the United States, and so frequent are the marriages of Canadian women to United States citizens, that the enactment of the Cable act by the United States congress has rendered many Canadian women stateless. A woman, who is a Canadian national, and who marries a citizen of the United States, does not now, by reason of such marriage become a citizen of the United States, although she thereby loses her status as a British subject.
There are at present hundreds of Canadian-born women who have lost Canadian nationality and who are no longer British subjects by reason of their marriage with citizens of the United States, although by such marriage they do not acquire United States citizenship. Such a woman-there are many hundreds of them in Canada, because if you will look at the statistics of marriage for the last few years you will find that many American citizens coming into our country and taking charge of large industrial institutions or being actively employed in the industrial life of this country, have married Canadian women- such a woman can no longer leave this country. She cannot obtain a passport from the United States authorities, because she is not a United States citizen; she cannot obtain a passport to go abroad from the Department of External Affairs of Canada, because she is no longer a British subject.
This matter was considered by a select committee of the parliament of the United Kingdom which was appointed in 1923 to consider the nationality of married women
who were formerly British subjects. Before that committee the representative of the British Foreign Office deprecated a change in the law which would result in varying nationalities in the same family, varying nationalities of husband and wife, varying nationalities also because the children under British law take the nationality of the father and not of the mother. The representative of the British Foreign Office before that committee expressed apprehension that such a change would inevitably lead to a demand for a change in the nationality of the children which, as I have said, now universally follows the nationality of the father. The British Foreign Office also urged the desirability of consulting and acting in concert in this matter with the self-governing dominions, and urged that no substantial change in the British law should be made without consultation with the dominions, and then only if the representatives of the dominions should concur in such change.
In order that the house may be aware of the varying arguments produced on that occasion I shall quote from the report of that committee, which by a majority vote approved of this particular section of the report, although as to the whole report there was a division of opinion.

To what committee is
my hon. friend referring?

To the special committee
of the parliament of the United Kingdom which met in 1923 to consider the effects of the enactment of the Cable act upon the nationality of women who before their marriage with Americans were British subjects. I am quoting from the report simply in order that the house may understand the arguments pro and con, because I do not regard this as a party measure; I think all measures of this kind should be generally accepted by the house. Section eleven of the report contains the following:
The committee as a result of this inquiry have come to the conclusion that a ease is not made out for a complete reversal of the principle governing the present law. They recognize the growing demand of many women anil of organized women's societies for equal rights with men in every respect, but they cannot overlook the fact that by marriage a woman is merged in the unlit of the family, and that within the family iit -is at present the husband who is head, who bears its legal responsibilities such as the maintenance ot the wife, the children and the home, and whose occupation in most cases is the decisive factor as to where that home is to be established, and who among other things gives his nationality to the children. It is their opinion, therefore, that in this important sphere of family life the nationality
8.%
Naturalization Act

of the husband should be the governing factor and determine the nationality of the wife. If two ride a horse one must ride in front.
The committee then proceeded to deal with one particular case, and to report specially thereon as follows:
There is one special ease, however, where in the opinion of the committee amendment of the law is required. It sometimes happens that through divergence in the larvs of states a woman finds herself through marriage deprived of the nationality of her parent state and not invested with the nationality of the state whose national she has married, e.g., a British woman to-day who marries a citizen of the United States under British law' loses her British nationality, but by virtue of the operation of the Cable act she does not acquire the nationality of the United States. This position of statelessness is undesirable and should be obviated by an amendment of the law to the effect that the woman shall not lose her original nationality if she does not acquire that of her husband under the law' of his country.
In the end the special committee of the parliament of the United Kingdom were equally divided with respect to the whole draft report from which I have quoted these two sections, which fairly express the ideas which prevailed in the minds of the majority of that committee.
This question came before the Imperial conference of 1026, and that conference deferred definite consideration of the matter of nationality of married women until the expert committee on inter-imperial relations might have an opportunity to report thereon. That committee met in October, 1029, and Canada was represented on the committee by the Minister of Justice in the late administration (Mr. Lapointe). After consideration that committee took no definite action. It is suggested to me that the reason for deferring definite consideration was due to the fact that on that occasion the government of the United Kingdom recommended that the matter be considered at an international conference on the ground that it was a proper subject for international agreement. Subsequently, at the Hague conference of I960, at w'hich Canada was represented, all the governments of the British commonwealth signed the Nationality convention, which was considered by that conference, and which contains the following articles:
Article 8. If the national law of the wife causes her to lose her nationality on marriage with a foreigner, this consequence shall be conditional on her acquiring the nationality of the husband.
Article 9. If the national law of the wife causes her to lose her nationality upon a change in the nationality of her husband occurring during marriage, this consequence shall be conditional on her acquiring her husband's new nationality.
[Mr. Calian.}
Article 10. Naturalization of the husband during marriage shall not involve a change in the nationality of the wife except with her consent.
These articles of the Hague international convention which met early in the year 1930 were considered at the last Imperial conference. Hon. members will have noticed that fact from the reports of that conference which have been laid upon the table of the house. The report of the Imperial conference of 1930 contains the following reference to this subject under the heading "Nationality of married women."
Careful consideration was given to the subject of the nationality of married women. All the members of the commonwealth represented at The Hague conference of 1930, signed the Nationality convention there concluded, and will, it is assumed, introduce such legislation as may be necessary to give effect to articles 8-10 of that convention. The conference was satisfied, however, that any proposals for the further modification of the principle of the existing law would fail to secure unanimous agreement. It followed that the conference was unable to make any recommendation for the substantive *amendment of the law on this subject except to the extent stated above.
This bill has been introduced to amend section 13 of the Naturalization Act, so as to incorporate therein the exceptions so approved at the Imperial conference, and to conform to those three articles of the Hague convention of 1930.
Will similar bills be introduced in various parliaments?

The governments of the
dominions were requested to introduce bills to carry out those provisions.
Practically the same as these.
I understand each government was requested to introduce a bill to carry out those provisions.
Practically the same as these?

I may say to the hon. gentleman that the bill before this house has been considered by the law officers of the Dominions Office in England. Since it has been introduced in this house there have been a few changes of verbiage which have 'been suggested and which I shall bring to the attention of the house at a later date. However in England they suggested no material amendments whatever since this bill was introduced. As there is a constitutional convention or understanding that amendments to the Naturalization Act defining the status of a British subject shall be made only by common consent of the dominions, the provisions of

Naturalization Act
this bill, as I repeat, have been restricted simply to carrying into effect the amendments which were agreed upon by the several dominions. I refer to such amendments as have now received approval in principle of the representatives of governments of the dominions, as well as the government of the United Kingdom. I think my predecessor in office will bear witness to the fact that when I assumed the office of Secretary of State there was a large volume of suggestions and recommendations from various women's associations throughout Canada for such an act as this. Those suggestions were not proceeded with for the reason that it was deemed advisable to have, first, an international agreement and, secondly, to have a common interimperial understanding with respect to the proposed amendments. These amendments are confined simply to the carrying into effect of the articles of the Hague conference which have been agreed upon by all parties. Since the bill has been introduced and distributed it has been discussed at length in many journals throughout the country. I have received a number of letters from various womens' organizations recommending that this principle, if I may so term it, be carried into effect. In their letters and resolutions they have not discussed with me the exact terminology of the bill, but there seems to be a general consensus of opinion, especially in the minds of women who take an active interest in public affairs, that such amendments should be made to the Naturalization Act of Canada. I repeat, I am simply submitting the bill for the careful consideration of members of this house. I think there might be some slight improvements made in the terminology, if the bill goes before a committee. To-day however I am merely dealing with the principle to which we have given effect in drafting the measure which is now submitted to the house.

May I be allowed to ask the hon. gentleman one or two questions. I would like him to elucidate one or two points. As I read it subsection 2 states:
A woman, having been a British subject, shall not be deemed to have ceased to be a British subject upon her marriage with an alien, except upon condition that in consequence of such marriage she acquire the nationality of her husband.
How would the hon. gentleman deal with the case of a woman acquiring by letters of naturalization the nationality of her husband in a foreign country? I refer to a British born woman.

My answer to that question is that under our law the moment a British 22110-57
subject acquires a certificate of naturalization under any foreign law and thereby becomes a subject or citizen of any foreign country he or she immediately thereupon ceases to be a British subject.

Would not subsection 2
have the effect of precisely curtailing that right of the woman to acquire another nationality by naturalization? It says here that a woman, upon certain conditions:
Except upon condition that in consequence of such marriage she acquires the nationality of her husband.
. . . remains a British subject. Therefore, under this section, if pleaded literally, her naturalization under the foreign law would not be acknowledged.
May I say to my hon. friend that I think the committee is the proper place to discuss that subject.
Quite true.

Furthermore although I
drafted this bill in conjunction with permanent officials of the Department of External Affairs I intend to suggest a very slight change in the first clause. My hon. friend will understand that upon reflection one may foresee technical difficulties which might arise. In the committee however I would prefer to entertain a discussion of such details.

Quite true. My other
question is this:	In the preparation of the
bill has consideration been taken of what will happen with regard to the children?
Under our law there is no doubt whatever that the children follow the nationality of the father. We have not interfered with that.

Mr. Speaker I do not intend to speak at length on the second reading of this bill, but I wish to say that I fully approve of the principle involved. Without referring particularly to the bill may I be permitted, in a very courteous way, to express regret that the practice of presenting bills followed in former sessions, has been discarded. It was the custom to place explanatory notes opposite to the sections of the bill giving in a summarized way the reasons for the proposals, and when a section was repealed to reproduce the text of such section. In the case of a new bill it was the practice to underline the new words in order to distinguish them from the paragraphs retained from the former act or bill. I think that might make the discussion of such technical matters as this easier for hon.

Naturalization Act

members. I am not speaking for myself; I have the documentation on these matters. I think the ministers themselves will find when they come to discuss the bill in committee that with the information I have referred to printed on the bill the discussion will be more relevant to the subject matter; otherwise questions will be put that have no bearing on the proposed amendments. I admit that in this instance the former section is practically repealed; in fact the whole section is changed and the words retained are not very material. But my remarks apply not only to this bill but to all bills introduced by the government, and which do not contain the explanatory notes and underlined changes as was the practice under the former government. I think the whole house will bear me out in my submission that this was a good practice and that it should not have been discontinued.
As to the bill itself, the Secretary of State has given the whole story of the change, and I think he has given it accurately. The question was raised in this house while I was in charge of the Department of State by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail), who made a motion in the session of 1927, asking the house to resolve that a woman of British nationality residing in Canada should not lose, or be deemed to lose, her nationality by the mere act of marriage with an alien, but that it should be open to her to make a declaration of alienage if she so desired. At the time I intimated, speaking for the government, that this was in full accordance with the policy of the government, but gave the reason-now given by my successor-that the delay then in taking action was due to the fact that the British citizenship recognized by the Naturalization Act is not confined to Canada but is empire-wide, and consequently there must be some degree of uniformity throughout the empire in order that British citizenship should be recognized internationally. The conditions for the obtaining of British citizenship were agreed upon by the different dominion governments and the government of the United Kingdom; that is, as to the number of years of residence, the character of the applicant, knowledge of official languages in the different parts of the empire where naturalization was sought, the desire to remain permanently within this or that part; there were also other matters such as this one regarding the status of British women marrying aliens, a status which was not altogether decided at the time. There was a series of conferences bringing no definite result. In 1926 it was decided, as the hon. Secretary of State has indicated, to leave the
[Mr Rinfret.]
matter over for an international conference, and later on for agreement between the different parts of the empire at the Imperial conference of 1930. I understand from what has been said this afternoon that an agreement has been finally reached, and that this bill incorporates the essentials of the agreement. I am glad to see the matter has been adjusted. I claim to be a feminist in my own province; there I am fighting the cause of feminism, and we hope that eventually success will crown our efforts. This I regard as another victory for the rights of women, and I think it will cure the very unsatisfactory condition of things that prevails where a British woman by marrying an alien loses her citizenship and does not acquire that of her husband.
But before I resume my seat I should like to direct the attention of the Secretary of State to another part of the Nauralization Act which might perhaps be amended at this time. In the interpretation section of the act will be found a definition of the word "disability", which I think is very unhappily phrased. It might have been warranted by the act as it now stands, but I do believe it should be changed if we adopt this bill. Paragraph (f) reads:
"Disability" means the status of being a married woman, or a minor, lunatic, or idiot.
The idea, of course, was to group together without what I may term any degree of relativity the different causes for disability. I think we should do away with this definition. It does not at all appeal to my sense of gallantry, and I think with the adoption of this bill it will become superfluous.
It had better be put into two sections, anyway.

I have not read through the bill to the extent of seeing if there remains any such disability with respect to married women, but I do submit to my hon. friend that if the disability of married women is removed by this measure, then, surely we should amend the definition.
The bill will be examined in committee, but with the principle of changing our act in order to meet the agreement arrived at in 1930 I am very fully in accord, and it was always the policy of the late government to work towards the achievement of such a position.

Mr. Speaker, I do not desire to delay the proceedings. I am quite in agreement with the principle of the bill, especially with regard to such Canadian women as marry American

Copyright Act
citizens, who, as the minister has stated, lose their British nationality and do not acquire that of their husbands. I can say that perhaps with great force because a condition of the kind arose in my own family; but of course that does not touch the question. My purpose in rising is to make an inquiry. I observe that under the bill a British woman marrying the citizen of a country which does not itself give her citizenship does not lose her British nationality. I wish to inquire whether, if she marries a citizen of a country in which she would acquire the national status of her husband, under this bill she might by her own act retain her British nationality?
Look at paragraph 3.

I do not think that covers it. I understand very well that a British woman marrying an alien does not lose her British citizenship if she does not acquire the citizenship of her husband; but if she does acquire his citizenship, can she by any act of her own retain her British status?
In any case, it seems to apply to only paragraph 3, that is, when the husband ceases to be a British subject during the marriage and not when the marriage takes place.
May I remind hon. members that the house is not yet in committee.
I presume my hon. friend will give attention to the proposal I made, with regard to the definition?

Certainly. I may say there have been a number of suggestions made by very learned lawyers in regard to this matter, and I should like an opportunity of considering them. The house may be assured that I will present them for consideration when we go into committee.

May I call my hon.
friend's attention to the fact that there is no explanatory note, as required by the rules of the house, in connection with this bill, and I see that the same thing occurs in connection with most of the bills which are on my file. These explanatory notes are required by the rules of the house, I understand, and they are very useful in the consideration and study of the bills.

That objection was raised by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), but I do not think there is any such rule. We are providing in this bill an entirely new section. I was under the impression that the law clerks were required to prepare the explanatory notes; perhaps I was under a 221X0-574
misapprehension. It may be my duty to do that, but I will look into it again, although in this case we are simply providing a new section.

May I make this suggestion? We are noit all lawyers in this chamber, and many private members who have not studied law find these explanatory notes very valuable. I know nothing about law, and if a short explanation appears I think it facilitates matters.

I think it is only just to my hon. friend the Secretary of State to say that his speech this afternoon upon the bill was the best explanatory note we have had for some time on these questions. I think he should be given credit for that.

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the Copyright Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to discuss this bill at length upon the second reading; I will merely make a few explanations. Every member of the house is well aware that in 1886 an international copyright union was established for the protection of literary and artistic property. A convention in that year was signed at Berne. This convention was revised at Paris in 1896 and again at Berlin in 1908, where the nations of Europe particularly were represented.
Then came a protocol which was signed at Berne in 1914, revising in certain particulars the anterior conventions. The original Berne convention of September 9, 1896, was signed by Great Britain on behalf of Canada and the other dominions. It was not until January 1, 1924, that the protocol signed at Berne was accepted by Canada on the initiative of the late government. The revised convention of November 13, 1908, however, was signed by the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland only on its own behalf. Canada was represented on that occasion and it was ratified on behalf of Canada on April 10, 1928. This convention was again revised at Rome on June 2, 1928. Canada was represented at Rome by Hon. Philippe Roy and Mr. John Desy, another gentleman from the office of the Canadian government in Paris, who signed the Rome convention on behalf of Canada.
The present bill has for one of its objects the granting of authority to the government of Canada to procure the ratification of that
Copyright Act

convention on behalf of the Canadian government. The time in which ratifications may be deposited at Rome expires on July 1, 1931. In order that Canada may adhere finally to the Rome convention it is necessary that certain definitions of our own act should be amended so as to bring the enforcement of the Rome convention within the terms of the principal clauses of our own act.
Then another matter is dealt with. My hon. friend from St. James (Mr. Rinfret), my predecessor in office, will recollect that while he was in office he received numerous protests from the various governments of Europe, from representative societies of authors throughout the world, and even from the Dominions Office in London, suggesting that section 40 of our act requiring compulsory registration of assignments of copyright could not possibly be carried out. That section requires that assignments of copyright should be registered by producing duplicate original copies. As a matter of fact many such assignments were made in one copy only; the assignors are long since dead, and it has been impossible therefore to prove title by such registration. Section 40 came up for decision in an Ontario case, that of the Canadian Performing Right Society versus the Famous Players Canadian Corporation, which case was carried to the privy council for decision and in which final judgment was rendered in 1927.
When I was in London during October and November, various delegations called upon me insisting that section 40 of our Act could not be complied with. They stated that if it were complied with it would bankrupt the societies which attempted to comply with it, and that it was not in strict conformity with the provisions of the Berne convention. For instance, it may not be known to hon. members that we have the Canadian Performing Right Society, which is organized under the Companies' Act, and which has its head office in the city of Toronto. That company controls between 2,000,000 and 2,500,000 copyrights, in respect of the right to perform those works. The registration by that company under section 40, involving a payment of $1 for each work registered, would impose a tax, as they call it, or would involve the payment of from $2,000,000 to $2,500,000 into the copyright office, a sum which I may say we would be very pleased to receive. But two sessions ago my predecessor introduced a bill to amend section 40, which received very general approval, I think, but which was not enacted owing to press of other work at the close of the session. I propose to repeal section 40 and to abolish compulsory registration of

copyright in Canada. But in doing so, there are certain conditions forced upon my attention with which I think we should deal. For instance, it is well known that Canadian authors find it advantageous to them to assign their copyright rights to American publishers. These assignments are made so as to cover not only the teritorial district of the United States, but some of them, by having sections introduced in the printed forms, as you see them sometimes on the back of an insurance policy, imply an assignment of the author's rights not only in respect of the territorial district of the United States but in respect of Canada as well. In fact, some of them which have come under my observation assign the author's rights in respect of the entire territory from the gulf of Mexico to the North Pole.
But our authors are sometimes not lawyers, sometimes not very practical business men; and in cases which have been brought to my attention they have, after making assignment of their rights for the whole continent to the American publisher, made a subsequent assignment of their rights to a Canadian publisher, which is confined to the territorial district of Canada. In that case there are conflicting assignments. It seems to me that those who wish to ascertain who has real title should be able to go to the copyright office in connection with the department of the Secretary of State and ascertain with whom they must deal with respect to such copyrights. I have therefore retained in the bill the provision that where an author assigns his right to copyright, and that assignment is registered voluntarily, at the copyright office, so long as that registration is extant it shall prevail over any other unregistered assignment which he has made. If any other assignee thinks that he has prior rights, then he can go to the courts and contest the issue and have that prior registration removed. AVe must protect the Canadian public to this extent, that if there are divergent rights which are irreconcilable in their terms, then the one who first registers his right shall, so far as the public is concerned, be deemed to have title.
There are certain other minor amendments made in the bill to bring it into closer conformity with the Rome convention. For instance, the Berne convention, and now the Rome convention also provides that in case of a joint authorship the copyright shall extend fifty years from the date of the death of the last of the joint authors. By, I suppose, some inadvertence we provided in our act that copyright should extend for fifty

Copyright Act
years from the death of the author who died first, and very considerable technical objections have been made by foreign governments and authors in foreign countries to this provision. We are now attempting to make our law conform to the convention to which we have subscribed.
Another important feature of this bill is found in the last section. This new section is introduced for the purpose of regulating the exercise of their monopoly by associations, societies and companies which carry on in Canada the business of acquiring, assigning and licensing performing rights in which copyright subsists. I have drafted that clause in ample terms with a view to its being considered by a select committee of this house in order that both parties to the controversy may have sufficient opportunity to present their views. I am overwhelmed with petitions and complaints from one end of Canada to the other that such performing right societies should be regulated. The general tenor of these complaints is this: that an author as an author should have a complete monopoly with respect to his work; that is, a monopoly created by statute. But when a thousand authors or the authors of a million works form a society and vest in that society title to all their works, then such monopoly, which can exist only by virtue of a statute, should be regulated with respect to its fees and lharges, exactly as a telephone company night be regulated.
I am simply giving the gist of the complaint. I am not saying that the Canadian Performing Right Society exacts fees and charges which are exorbitant. But their contracts must be signed by the hotel companies, because they cannot perform a musical work in any hotel, from the Atlantic to the Pacific unless they have a licence from the performing right society. And it is alleged that the contract so far pressed upon their attention is a contract, not for the right to perform a single, individual work, but a contract to perform the whole two million or two and a half million works which this society controls.
I have received protests from representatives of the Canadian Pacific Railway with respect to their radio performances, and protests from the Canadian National Railways as well. I have received protests from nearly every large radio broadcasting concern in Canada. There must be a general discussion before that select committee as to the special measures to be taken to prevent a monopoly of that character from making undue exactions from the Canadian people.

I have just received a
protest from a parish priest with regard to presentations which are made for charitable purposes. Would it be possible to amend the act to provide that no fee shall be paid in the case of performances given for charitable purposes?
There is one clause dealing definitely with that aspect of the matter.
Thank you.

I am making no charge or
complaint against the Canadian Performing Right Society. But it is represented to me that in many districts in Canada which are more or less isolated-for instance, in northern Ontario and in certain parts of Quebec-community centres are formed, usually about the parish church, or around the local band or community choir, and during the winLcr they hold three or four entertainments 1o provide funds for a community hall, perhaps, or to maintain some other community undertaking. They charge fifteen, or twenty, or twenty-five cents for children and sometimes as high as fifty cents for adults, and the fund so raised is used for community purports. There is hardly one of these entertainment;] that does not perform through the village choir or through the village band, two or three or more of these musical works, the copyright to which is vested in a Canadian or foreign copyright society or association. I do not know about the truth of the charge, but it is suggested to me that from time to time, when such community entertainments are held, persons who are or who purport to be agents of such societies intimate to the village choir or to the village band that unless they pay performing rights fees to such a society, they will be haled under our law before a magistrate, or they will be brought up in court and compelled to pay. With that in view I have introduced a clause which may be too broad, but which is the clause to which I just referred my hon. friend. It is clause 11 which reads:
Nothing contained in the Copyright Act nor in this act shall be construed to prohibit the performance of any musical works in which copyright subsists by churches, colleges, schools, or by philanthropic, charitable or fraternal organizations, provided the performance is given for religious, educational, benevolent or charitable purposes.
That may be too broad. It has been suggested to me by some who are interested in performing rights that I should introduce there the words "provided the performance is given gratuitously," but such matters must be dealt with by the select committee after

hearing the evidence. Therefore I submit the bill for the favourable consideration of the house, and if it passes its second reading I shall move that it be referred to a select committee, of which the names of the members comprising it have been agreed upon by the whips of the several parties.

Inasmuch as this bill is going before a special committee, I shall not endeavour to discuss it to-day. I wish, however, to point out that the second reading of a bill always involves the adoption of a principle. There are two schools of thought regarding copyright and from that duality comes the whole difficulty about having the proper distinction. One school of thought, which is the European school, is that copyright is a right in itself; that whenever a writer has composed, or a painter or whoever he is has created a work, he has the full ownership of that work in using the copyright. That is the conception adopted by all European countries which formed the convention in Berne, later on confirmed in Rome, whereby in every country in that union the mere fact that a person was the composer or writer of a book gave him the fullest rights as to all the copyright privileges that might be attached to it.
That is the claim of the authors.

Yes. The other school of thought is what I shall call the United States school of thought, which says that copyright is a privilege -and can be enjoyed only if it is registered. In the United States of America a copyright will not be recognized unless it has been properly registered. From that duality arises the whole difficulty to which the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) has alluded, and protests, sometimes from the north and sometimes from the south, have always accompanied any attempt to legislate in regard to this matter.
Whilst I was listening to my hon. friend I thought he was endeavouring to write my own biography. It is true that as a member, and later on as a minister, I tried to introduce and I did introduce legislation, the latest bill being I think in 1930, doing away with section 40. My bon. friend is right when he says that a whole group of societies and institutions were once elated over the fact that the government had decided to introduce a bill of that kind; but when he said that it was due to pressure of work that the bill was dropped or not proceeded with, he did not give the complete story. There were protests from innumerable societies, church societies, charitable institutions and also performers and

publishers, representing that we were going too far and that it was not fair to them to grant copyright without any registration whatever.
The point I wish to make to-day is that we shall have to make our choice. We must have in this country copyright legislation which will be clear-cut. Either we shall adhere to the convention of Rome and do away with registration, or we shall withdraw from Rome and have our own registration. We have been hesitating-and I will take my share of the blame for that if parliament so desires- we have been going from one point to the other, listening to protests first on one side and then on the other. I surmise from this bill, which is somewhat more extensive than, but in principle very much along the line of the bill which I introduced last session, that the policy of the present government is to have our copyright legislation in conformity with the decisions reached in Rome. It is on that understanding that I shall agree to the second reading of the bill being passed to-day, -but I know very well when we get into committee we shall hear representations from all sides and every effort will be made by the usual people who come around when copyright is being discussed, to prevent the bill from coming back from the committee and the committee from reaching a final decision. I hope the government intends to proceed with the bill to the fullest extent. It is hard to say what the Senate will do with it later on.
I wish to insist upon this point, because it has been the whole crux of the difficulty in the past; we must make up our minds whether we wish to deal with copyright as the European countries do and do away -with registration, following the convention strictly without any reservation, or not. If we wish to follow the convention, I believe there are in the bill certain sections which we shall have to drop in order to put our legislation into full conformity with the decisions of Rome.
We do not recognize the decisions of Rome.

I say: If we fail to do that, then we shall have to withdraw from the convention and have our own registration, a very improper course, I think. I have been trying very hard from year to year to achieve the purpose which my hon. friend says he has in mind now. He can count upon my fullest cooperation, but I know on both sides of the house there are members who will not be with us, and we might as well make up our minds that by the first of July we must give our adherence or withdraw it.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF PROVINCIAL COMPENSATION ACTS TO ALL GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES

speechtext:
Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Government Employees Compensation Act to extend the benefits of the act to all employees in the service of His Majesty excepting those for whom provision is made under other statutes, and to extend the interpretation of the term "compensation" to include any benefits, expenses or allowances that are provided for under provincial compensation acts.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Maloney in the chair.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF PROVINCIAL COMPENSATION ACTS TO ALL GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution is for the purpose of amending the Government Employees' Compensation Act so that provincial compensation acts will apply to all government employees. At the present time in the various provinces the law varies. For instance, postal employees are covered in the provinces of Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia only; customs officers are covered in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia only; lighthouse keepers and employees on boats carrying supplies to lighthouses or attending to aids to navigation are not covered in Nova Scotia. Some of the provincial compensation acts do not apply to government employees in the various departments; they may cover those engaged in some industry, but the courts rule that the government service is not an industry. The purpose of the bill to be introduced, based on the resolution, is to briDg all employees of the government under the various provincial compensation acts. It is expected that this will cost the government an additional $70,-
000.

I would like to direct the attention of the minister to a matter which I have taken up privately with the Minister of Marine, and I hope the minister will take this opportunity to remedy a grievance which exists in British Columbia between his department and the local provincial authorities over the interpretation of the word "employee". A very simple change in the interpretation would remedy the situation.
Here is the difficulty: Lighthouse keepers, of course, are paid by the Department of Marine, and there is an arrangement under which certain lighthouse keepers employ assistants. The department is either too economical or too mean to pay the wages of the second man, so they have an arrangement whereby the lighthouse keeper must employ an assistant, for whom he is allowed a few hundred dollars extra. They do not allow a living wage for a man but only about half that wage, and they sanction the practice, which is often followed by lighthouse keepers, of employing their wives or junior members of their families to do the work, which really is not the full work of a man. Occasionally, where there are two or three assistants, they do pay a full wage for the assistant, but here is the situation: It is held by the Workmen's Compensation Board that this assistant is an employee of this government, inasmuch as he is paid indirectly by the government. There can be no question about that, with the record of wages paid to lighthouse keepers showing that when an assistant is necessary a considerably larger amount is paid. The Workmen's Compensation Board of British Columbia have always held in that case that the assistant was the employee of the government, but the Marine department have held that he was an employee of the lighthouse keeper. The result is that if an accident of that kind happens, the lighthouse keeper is of course quite unalble to meet any claim against him, and there is therefore considerable criticism of the government. It is claimed that they are cheaply avoiding at least a moral responsibility by not paying out this sum to the injured workman. The trouble could be avoided very simply by having a change in the interpretation of the word " employee " so as to cover a case of that kind. The other case to which I wish to allude is similar. In certain cases the Public
Works department does work by day labour, employing teams. These teams and their drivers may be taken off a farm in the vicinity at a time when they are not busy. The Workmen's Compensation Board of British Columbia does not apply to farmers, and the department here-possibly the Justice department-have ruled that in that case a man working as a teamster by the day on some clearing, or perhaps road making for some Dominion department, is not an employee of the government but is a farmer, or an employee of a farmer, although he is at the moment working not as a farmer but as a professional teamster for the government. That also is a case in which a rather cheap argument is used to withhold compensation from the man injured in that capacity. I understand that the act that governs this provides its own interpretation of the word employee, so that if the interpretation were changed along the lines I suggest it would not conflict with the meaning of the word employee as contained in any other act such as the Civil Service Act. " Employee " could be made to cover, amongst others, the two classes I have mentioned. I trust the minister will look into this before the bill is brought down, because it would remove a very real injustice. I do not think the Marine department would like to have it said that they were purposely unjust. I know of one case where a man risked his life and suffered considerable injury from fire to save the lighthouse property; but because he was an assistant to the lighthouse keeper in that technical sense of the word he was told to look to the lighthouse keeper as his direct employer if he wished compensation. Of course, the lighthouse keeper had no funds with which to compensate him. If the change were made as I suggest, it would do justice to a class of people, particularly lighthouse keepers, who are not overpaid as it is.

The observations of the right hon. gentleman are certainly worthy of very careful consideration. The government has considered the matter. I am sure that the right hon. gentleman would say that we considered it when the government was formed, but I hasten to tell him that there is no intention to impose upon the Prime Minister the Finance department as well as others and thereby reduce the number of portfolios, although the arrangement so far has resulted in a substantial saving of money. The matter is under consideration. I think that some of the departments, in view of the change that has been brought about by reason of the resources being turned over to the western provinces, might be consolidated. The right hon. gentleman has had ten years of very considerable experience; I recall quite clearly the effort he made to reduce the number of portfolios, but in the end he found it necessary to increase them. The recommendations of the Duncan report with resnect to the fisheries was responsible, not wholly, but practically, for the creation of one new department, if the administration was to give effect, as was intended, to the report.

Salaries Act
I have had in mind for some time that this country should have a department of communications. I have thought about it a very great deal. There is the air, there is radio, wireless and cable communication

Yes, post office, railways and other forms of communication. I have given some thought to the matter but obviously, for reasons which the right hon. gentleman understands and the house appreciates, I have been only a few months in Canada since undertaking this task and I have not had as much time to consider the matter as I should like. But what has been said to-night by the right hon. gentleman I shall be very glad indeed to take in the spirit in which it is offered, as giving his benediction to the efforts we are making to improve the public service, and if the results to be obtained can best be secured by the methods suggested we shall not hesitate to apply them.
I hope within the next few days to introduce a bill mentioned in the speech from the throne, which I can anticipate to this extent, that it will make for more efficient control with respesct to our revenues and expenditures. I happen to know of my own knowledge that the right hon. gentleman himself bestowed considerable thought to the matter.
I am very glad that the committee has taken the view it has in the discussion we are now having; for, after all, at the beginning of this century the revenues of Canada were only $50,000,000. When Sir John Macdonald died the revenues were $37,000,000. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier went out of office in 1911 my memory is that the total revenues of this country, just a little time before that, crossed the $100,000,000 mark. Now they approximate, at the least, $1,000,000 a day, and the extent to which consolidation of departments would improve the public service is a matter that I am not prepared to speak about at the moment because I have not arrived at a definite conclusion. In a country as vast as Canada it is very difficult to say, where you have revenues of approximately $1,000,000 a day to be dealt with, that you are making for efficiency by imposing too much detail upon him who administers. When the chief administrative officer is unable at a glance to know the state of efficiency with which the details of government are carried on by those in the departments, there is failure; and if you have too large a responsibility on the one individual the data comes before him too much in tabloid form to
make possible an efficient working of the machinery. The effort that my colleagues and myself are endeavouring to make at the moment is to utilize the experience of the past in the light of the knowledge of to-day and to accomplish just what the right ^ hon. gentleman has in mind, namely, efficiency in the conduct of the public service.

I wish simply
to correct one impression which my right hon. friend has left with the committee. It is true that, for the reason mentioned, the late administration did, in its last year of office, add one portfolio through the separation of the departments of fisheries and marine. But it is also true that when we came into office we made two or three very imporant consolidations. For instance, there was the Department of Inland Revenue, the Department of Customs, each presided over by a separate minister, and there was a separate branch of the public service dealing with the income tax. Those three were brought into the one department of National Revenue. Similarly, when we came into office, there was the Department of Militia and Defence, the Department of the Naval Service, and a separate air board. Those three were brought together into one department, that of National Defence.
